This report is a structural snapshot of a software codebase. It shows what languages are used, what the main building blocks are, what outside packages the project relies on, and where the program starts running. Use it to onboard a new contributor, share a high-level overview with stakeholders, or audit how a project is organized. A glossary at the end explains any technical terms.

System architecture

How the system fits together

One map of the whole system: the product's own modules (vendored and third-party code is excluded) arranged in tiers — user-facing code on top, server code in the middle, data stores at the bottom. Dashed lines are HTTP calls from the frontend to a backend module, solid lines are code imports, and coloured lines into cylinders show which service writes to which store. Modules marked with ▸ are entry points — the doors through which requests arrive. Solid lines are code imports; the dependency matrix further down shows the full import detail.

The product is 7 frontend modules, 28 backend modules, 4 data stores, connected by 8 HTTP call paths.

Languages

Programming languages are the rules and vocabulary used to write code. A codebase usually has one primary language plus several supporting ones (configuration files, documentation, build scripts).

Click any language marked with a ▸ to see what it is, where it usually runs, and the role it tends to play in a codebase.

LanguageFilesLinesShare
▸TypeScript27954,00435.8%
Frontend · backend

JavaScript plus a type system that catches mistakes before the code runs. Used wherever JavaScript is, but favoured for larger apps and teams because the types document intent and prevent whole classes of bugs. Compiles down to plain JavaScript.

▸JSON1533,74822.4%
Data · config

A simple, language-neutral format for structured data. In a codebase it shows up as configuration files, package manifests, fixtures, and the payloads most web APIs send and receive. Data, not code.

▸HTML4116,98911.3%
Markup · frontend

The markup language that defines the structure of a web page — headings, paragraphs, links, forms, images. It describes what is on the page; CSS controls how it looks and JavaScript makes it interactive. Not a programming language in the usual sense, so it carries no logic to trace.

▸Markdown4115,29110.1%
Docs

A lightweight plain-text format for writing formatted documents — READMEs, docs, notes — that converts cleanly to HTML. Its presence usually signals documentation rather than application code.

▸Python7112,6958.4%
Backend · data · scripting

A general-purpose language known for clean, readable syntax. In most codebases it lives on the backend — powering web APIs and services — or off to the side running data analysis, AI/ML, automation, and build scripts. It almost never runs in the browser.

▸YAML1010,1276.7%
Config

A human-friendly configuration format. Heavily used for CI/CD pipelines, container orchestration (Kubernetes), and tool settings. Lots of YAML usually means substantial automation or deployment config.

▸Shell163,8682.6%
Scripting · ops

Command-line scripts (Bash, Zsh, etc.) used for automation, setup steps, and glue between programs. Usually part of build pipelines and developer tooling rather than the product itself.

▸SQL71,9991.3%
Data · database

The language for querying and manipulating relational databases. Not general-purpose — it expresses what data to read or change, which the database engine then carries out.

▸JavaScript91,3770.9%
Frontend · backend

The native language of the web browser, and — through Node.js — a popular backend language too. In a typical codebase it drives interactive frontend behaviour and/or server-side APIs. The most widely deployed language in the world.

▸CSS23920.3%
Styling · frontend

The styling language of the web — colours, layout, spacing, fonts, animation. It decides how the HTML structure actually looks and adapts across screen sizes. Pure presentation; it contains no program logic.

▸TOML21870.1%
Config

A configuration format chosen for being easy to read and unambiguous. Common in Rust (`Cargo.toml`) and Python (`pyproject.toml`) projects to declare settings and dependencies.

▸Makefile11440.1%
Build

A build-automation format that defines named tasks (build, test, clean) you run with `make`. Old but durable; often the front door to a project's common commands.

▸Dockerfile2700.0%
Build · ops

A recipe for building a container image — a self-contained package of an app plus the operating system and dependencies it needs to run identically anywhere. Its presence means the project is meant to be containerised and deployed.

Top-level modules

A module is a self-contained folder of related code that handles one job. Modules relate to one another by importing each other — one module calls into another to reuse what it already does, and that wiring is exactly what the dependency matrix further down maps out.

The folders below are this codebase’s top-level modules — the primary areas that do the heavy lifting, sitting near the top of the directory tree rather than buried as small helpers deep inside it. They’re the right altitude for a first read: enough to see the system’s shape without getting lost in every nested file.

Dependency graph

How the modules connect

Each row and column is a module. A coloured cell at row A, column B means A imports from B — darker cells mean more imports flow that way. Modules are grouped by service (the coloured bands on the edges), with each service's modules sorted from largest to smallest. A clean codebase shows tight blocks along the diagonal (each service mostly depends on itself); off-diagonal blocks indicate cross-service coupling. The pale grey diagonal just marks where each module sits — modules don't import themselves.

42 import relationships were detected, all of them staying inside a single service. Visually that’s the block-diagonal pattern below — a sign of clean service boundaries.

This matrix maps code imports, so it only parses languages that have them — here, Python, TypeScript. These were also found but sit outside the import map: HTML, JSON, Markdown, SQL, Shell, YAML. Those are configuration, data, markup, documentation, and styling formats; they don’t express module-to-module code dependencies, so feeding them into this diagram would add noise rather than signal.

Observations
  • admin in Back-End-FitTalk imports from 5 other modules — the highest fan-out in the codebase. Watch for god-module drift.
  • prisma in Back-End-FitTalk is depended on by 13 other modules — any change here ripples widely; treat as a stable interface.
  • Zero cross-service imports were detected — services are fully decoupled at the file level. Network calls (see the topology section) are the only inter-service contract.
  • prisma is a utility hub — 13 modules depend on it. Strong consistency benefit; also a single point of churn when its API evolves.

Service topology

How the services talk to each other

Each card is a separately-deployable service — its own app or process, with its own deployment lifecycle. The coloured strip across the top and the badge in the corner tell you what kind of service it is (frontend, backend, worker, …). The arrows between cards are HTTP calls aggregated across every route the source service makes to the target — the number on each arrow is the total call count, so thicker arrows mean heavier traffic. Where the matrix above showed file-level imports inside services, this view shows the conversation between services across the network.

3 services form a linear chain: Front-End-FitTalk → Back-End-FitTalk → FitTalk_AI. Front-End-FitTalk drives the bulk of the traffic with 54 calls to its downstream.

Click a service or a flow to isolate it · Esc clears

16 outbound HTTP calls couldn't be matched to a known endpoint — likely external APIs, dynamic URLs, or routes the scanner didn't pick up. They're not drawn above.

Observations
  • Back-End-FitTalk sits on 2 of the 2 call edges — it's the network hub. Loss of this service breaks the most flows.
  • 98% of all inter-service traffic flows on a single edge: Front-End-FitTalk → Back-End-FitTalk. That edge is the system's primary failure-correlation surface.
  • 2 server frameworks are in use (FastAPI, NestJS) — heterogeneous, meaning observability, middleware, and request-handling conventions differ per service.
  • 16 outbound HTTP calls didn't resolve to a known endpoint — likely external APIs, dynamic URLs, or routes the scanner missed. They aren't drawn in the diagram.

Request flow

What happens when a request flows through

Where the diagrams above show structure, this one shows behaviour — what happens when a request flows through the system. Each row is one entry-point module: the caller(s) on the left, the module receiving the request in the middle, that module's key code dependencies, and the data store the flow ultimately writes to on the right. Reading top-to-bottom gives you a near-complete map of which HTTP surfaces exist in this codebase and how each one connects all the way down to persistence.

16 entry-point modules expose HTTP endpoints in this codebase. The rows below trace each one from caller to data store; 8 have a complete caller→deps→store chain detected.

Observations
  • nutrition in Back-End-FitTalk exposes 20 HTTP endpoints — the largest single attack surface in this codebase.
  • 7 entry modules (admin, ai-coaching, support, goals) have no detected callers in this codebase — either called from outside (mobile apps, webhooks, scheduled jobs) or dead code worth confirming.
  • 13 of the 16 entry modules depend on prisma — a strong consistency win, but any breaking change to prisma ripples across most of the HTTP surface.
  • Every traced flow ultimately writes to POSTGRES — uniform persistence makes reasoning about transactions easier, but also means the database is the single point of contention under load.
  • Only 39 of 135 endpoints (29%) were matched to a caller in the scan — most endpoints have no detected internal client, suggesting external callers (mobile/web apps) or unscanned consumers.

Data lineage

Where each service stores its data

Where does each service store its data? Cards on the left are services; the cylinders on the right are data stores — the universal database glyph. The weighted ribbon between a service and a store is sized by the number of distinct data models (database tables, document types, etc.) declared via that service's ORM. Stores drawn at reduced opacity were detected in environment config but have no ORM model declarations — they're typically accessed via raw client libraries (Redis SDK, Firebase Admin, etc.) rather than through an ORM.

2 services persist data to 1 store via Prisma, SQLAlchemy. The largest footprint is Back-End-FitTalk with 61 models in PostgreSQL. 3 additional stores are referenced in env config but no ORM models link to them.

Observations
  • 100% of modeled writes go to PostgreSQL — the primary data store. No read replica or write/cache split was detected at the ORM level.
  • 2 services write to PostgreSQL (Back-End-FitTalk, FitTalk_AI) — shared ownership of a data store. Watch for schema-coupling and migration coordination overhead.
  • 3 stores (Supabase, Redis, Firebase / Firestore) are referenced in env config but no ORM models declare them — direct client-library usage. Add coverage by inspecting the matching service's source for the relevant SDK calls.
  • 2 ORM frameworks are in use (Prisma, SQLAlchemy) — different migration paths, different schema-evolution tooling per service.

Glossary

Plain-English definitions for the technical terms used above. Only includes entries relevant to what was found in this codebase.

Concepts
Module
A self-contained folder of related code that handles one responsibility — for example an 'auth' module handles login, a 'billing' module handles payments. Most codebases split work into modules so contributors can focus on one area at a time.
Package
A piece of reusable code published by someone else that this codebase depends on. Adding a package is faster and safer than re-writing the same code from scratch.
Dependency
An external package this project needs to run. The dependency listing is essentially the project's shopping list of outside code.
Entry point
The specific file the program starts running from when launched. Languages have different conventions: Python uses `main.py`, JavaScript uses `index.js`, Go uses `main.go`, Rust uses `main.rs`.
Manifest
A small file at the project's root that declares its dependencies and metadata. Examples: `package.json`, `requirements.txt`, `Cargo.toml`, `go.mod`.
LOC (Lines of code)
A rough size indicator — *not* a quality measure. A 100-LOC module isn't necessarily worse than a 1,000-LOC one. Use LOC for orientation, not judgement.
Source root
A directory holding the main program code, kept separate from configuration, tests, and build artifacts. Common names: `src`, `lib`, `app`, `cmd`, `pkg`.
Service
An independently deployable unit of code — its own app, its own process, its own deploy. A monorepo can hold many services (e.g. one for the mobile app, one for the backend API, one for the AI worker). Services talk to each other over the network, not by importing each other's code.
Endpoint
A specific URL a service responds to, paired with an HTTP method. `GET /api/v1/users/:id` is an endpoint. Services advertise endpoints; other services call them.
ORM (Object-Relational Mapper)
A library that lets you read and write database rows using normal code objects instead of writing SQL by hand. Popular ORMs: Prisma (TS), SQLAlchemy (Python), Mongoose (Mongo), ActiveRecord (Ruby).
Data store
A place where data persists between requests. Databases (Postgres, MySQL, Mongo), caches (Redis), and object storage (S3, MinIO) are all data stores.
Topology
The shape of a system — which pieces exist and how they connect. A topology diagram answers "what's deployed and what talks to what."
Vendored
Third-party code copied directly into this repository instead of installed from a package registry. Vendored folders ship with the project but aren't part of its own product code, so the report shows them faded. Teams vendor a library to pin an exact version, patch it locally, or keep building when the upstream package isn't available — but it becomes code you now carry and maintain.
Tools, libraries & services
FastAPI
A modern Python framework for building web APIs quickly, with automatic validation and interactive documentation.
NestJS
A structured, opinionated framework for building Node.js backend applications in TypeScript.
Programming languages
CSS
The styling language of web pages — controls colors, layout, fonts, and animations.
Dockerfile
A set of instructions for building a container image. A container packages an app with its OS and dependencies so it runs identically anywhere.
HTML
The markup language of web pages — defines the structure of a page (headings, paragraphs, links, images).
JSON
A data format used to send structured data between systems. Most web APIs speak JSON.
JavaScript
The programming language of the web — runs in every browser. Also runs servers (via Node.js). The most widely used language on the planet.
Makefile
A build script format. Defines named tasks (build, test, clean) that you run with `make <task>`. Old but still widely used.
Markdown
A lightweight format for writing formatted text. Used for READMEs, documentation, and notes. Compiles to HTML.
Python
A general-purpose programming language known for readable syntax. Popular for scripting, data analysis, AI/ML, web backends, and automation.
SQL
The language used to query and manipulate databases. Stands for Structured Query Language.
Shell
Scripting language for the command line (Bash, Zsh, etc.). Used for automation, build steps, and glue code between programs.
TOML
A configuration format chosen for readability. Used by Rust's Cargo, Python's pyproject.toml, and others.
TypeScript
A programming language that adds type checking on top of JavaScript. Popular for web frontends, Node.js servers, and large applications where catching bugs before running the code matters.
YAML
A human-readable data format. Used heavily for configuration files in CI/CD, Kubernetes, and modern dev tooling.
